title: Do open permit records predict how long a permit and the build behind it take, better than each city's own averages?
lede: research programme: LightGBM quantile models beat the per-city, per-type empirical-quantile baseline on pinball loss in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells (2024 test year, Chicago, San Francisco, Austin); Chicago's tails are the exception
summary: An open research programme on duration forecasting from public building-permit feeds. Session 1 wrote the proposal (12 checked works, four falsifiable hypotheses, time-split evaluation with conformal intervals) and probed the feeds: Chicago has 851,778 rows, all issued, so it cannot show permits never issued; San Francisco has 1,297,657 rows with 750,188 completed; Austin has 2,382,939 rows with 2,184,191 completed. NYC DOB NOW is excluded until its licence is checked. Session 2 built the loader, schema, datasheets and a manifest (row counts match the probe) and found the median application-to-issue lag is 0 days in all three cities (p90 56, 81, 142), with SF and Austin build times at a median of about 105 days. Session 5 ran the reference-class baselines on the real feeds; session 6 (milestone 3) fitted LightGBM quantile models (q 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) and a same-day classifier, forward split with train to 2022 and early stopping on 2023, tested on 2024. The boosted model beats the baseline in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells by 2 to 36% (paired week-block bootstrap intervals exclude zero); in Chicago application-to-issue it wins at the median and loses at the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles. One test year, 3 seeds, fixed fast configuration, intervals not yet conformalised.
